Text.Text: Table's clean, the board's empty, and I'm back to dealing for fun. Aces and eights ride with you now. Pull up a chair anytime; first round's on the house you beat.
Easy, friend. This table has a buy-in, and it's everything that pistol can teach you. You're still learning the deck. Come back when there's nothing left in it you haven't drawn.

Here's a card, face-down. Yours the day you earn a look at it. Now the game. Somebody's dealing my hand down in that canyon: my old table, my marked deck, and six eager adepts learning to shoot like me and cheat like them. Fold all six and bring me the Dead Man's Hand Canyon Range Tally they keep count on. I like an honest pot.
There's the spirit. Gate key's yours. Don't count the pot before the sixth card falls.

The draw you make when you're already beaten. The table says you're dead, everyone's counting their winnings, and your hand moves anyway. It isn't luck, friend. It's refusing to die on someone else's count.
Right down there. My key opens the marshal's gate at the canyon mouth; past it, the house rules are theirs. Long walk, bad light, worse company. Play accordingly.
Six adepts holding low pairs and betting like aces. They'll crowd you, all smiles and spread fingers. Smile back. Then take the pot one hand at a time.
Six adepts, one tally, and the pot's still sitting in the canyon. Hands don't fold themselves, friend.
Word travels fast at a small table. Six players left the game feet-first. Let's see that tally.
All there, honest to the last line. Take your cut. And that face-down card of yours? It just got interesting.

The adepts were the ante. Now the sharps: five specialists who turned my sightline calibrator into a stacked deck. Long lanes, patient triggers, every angle pre-dealt. Bust all five and bring me the Dead Man's Hand Sightline Calibrator before they mark the whole canyon.
Five sharps, long lanes, one honest gun. I like those odds. They shouldn't.

Mine, once. I dealt at that range for years and taught the draw to anyone whose credits were good. A few of them had good credits and bad hearts. They kept my deck, marked every card in it, and now they deal my game to killers. A man should retire his own deck. I intend to.
On the market, a stack of credits. To them, every rigged angle in the canyon. To me, the difference between a duel and an execution. I've dealt both, friend. Only one of them lets me sleep.
Patient. A sharp never bets early. They'll let you walk the long lanes thinking the table's cold, then show the whole hand at once. Make them bet first. Then raise.
Five sharps still working the long lanes, and my calibrator's still marking their cards. The game's waiting on you, friend.
Five sharps busted and the canyon's odds gone honest. The calibrator, if you please.
Clean deck, honest table. You play tighter than you did. The house upstairs has noticed, which is bad news and good news. Mostly bad. Around here that means interesting.

Now the pit boss. The warden holds the deep range, wears the house crest, and decides who plays and who pays. Best hand at that table and he knows it, which is his tell. Break him and bring me the Dead Man's Hand Shattered Range Crest when it cracks. One rule from me, house law: stake two friends and sit down as three. The house folds to a full hand. It eats a lone ace.
A full hand against the pit boss. That's a game I'd pay to watch. Don't make me pay for anything else.

He ran security at my table before he ran the table itself. Never bluffs, never tilts, never draws first, and he's never needed to draw twice. That crest used to mean the range was safe. Now it means the range is his.
Past the marshal's gate, follow the firing line down until the walls close in. That pit is his seat, picked years ago: worst light for you, best for him. He'll be in it.

Because I've staked lone aces against him before, friend, and paid for three funerals out of my own winnings. Cards don't beat the warden. Numbers do. Three guns, three angles, and his perfect hand is suddenly playing the whole table.
The warden's still holding the deep range and his crest is still in one piece. Gather your three, friend. The pot doesn't split for effort.
The pit boss, busted at his own table. I'd have paid for a seat at that one. Show me the crest.
Shattered. Couldn't have cracked it cleaner myself. The deep range just lost its house edge, and somewhere upstairs a man is counting his chips and coming up short.

Four players left at the high table: the inner circle. They bank the whole operation, and they hold a marshal's challenge chit, the old kind, the kind that buys a seat across from the man who runs it all. Clear all four chairs and bring me the Dead Man's Hand Marshal's Challenge Chit. It's the buy-in for the last game.
Clear the chairs, lift the chit, and don't scratch it. It's the most honest thing left in that canyon.

Two killers, a bookkeeper who shoots better than the killers, and the woman who marked my deck in the first place. They've banked every crooked game down there for years. Nothing moves without their cut.

Old range law, friend. Lay that chit on the marshal's table and the marshal must play you. No guards, no tolls, no folding. The man upstairs holds my old title and hasn't honored a chit in years. We're going to make him.
As a syndicate. Four hands, one pot, and they'll spend each other's lives before their own. Bring the same two who watched your back in the pit. Four against three is closer odds than they'd like.
Four chairs at the high table are still warm, and the chit's still in their bank. The last game can't start without the buy-in, friend.
High table's empty and the bank is open. Hand it over. Let's see the buy-in.
One marshal's chit, paid in full. I'll post the challenge myself; answering it is the one law even he kept. Sleep, eat, kiss whoever you kiss. The last hand gets dealt when you're ready.

Challenge posted, challenge answered. Now the truth, friend. The man up there holds the real Dead Man's Hand: the draw that comes after he's beaten, the hand you can't fold against. I dealt it to him myself, back when he was mine to teach, and he has never lost with it. Go to the overlook and take it from him. And hear me plain: nobody plays the master heads-up and cashes out. Bring your two. Full hand or no hand.
Three players, one last pot. Whatever happens up there, it's been a pleasure staking you.

My partner, once. We dealt that range together and split every pot even. Then I caught him dealing seconds to a boy who died of it, and I walked. He kept the table, the title, and the hand I taught him. That pot's been sitting there for years, friend. I'm finally calling.
The marshal's overlook, top of the range, where the challenge board hangs. He'll honor the chit in the open. Style matters to him. It's the last honest thing in the man.

You'll put him down, and his hand will move anyway. That's the trick of it, the draw that comes after the beating. First time you see it, you freeze. So don't be the only one at the table. Three guns means when that dead hand moves, somebody's already answering.
The marshal's still at the overlook holding the last hand, and challenges don't expire. You might, friend, so take your two along and finish the game.
The canyon went quiet an hour ago. Quiet like a table after last call. Tell me how the hand played.

Then turn over the card I dealt you. Aces and eights, friend. The dead man's hand, held by somebody still breathing. That's the whole lesson, and it's yours now, along with the pay and my marker: any table I sit at, you have a seat.
Back to the game.
Deal me in. Six folds, one tally.
What exactly is the Dead Man's Hand?
Where's this table of yours?
What are the adepts holding?
I'll pass this hand.
Six folds. Here's their count.
Back to the sharps.
Five sharps. I'll bring your calibrator.
Whose game is this, really?
What's the calibrator worth?
How do the specialists play?
I'm sitting this one out.
Your calibrator. The deck's clean.
Back to the pit boss.
Three of us, then. The pit boss busts.
What do you know about the warden?
Where's the deep range?
Why three? I've done fine alone.
I fold. For now.
His crest. It didn't survive the last round.
Back to the high table.
Four chairs. I'll clear the table.
Who sits at the high table?
What does the chit buy, exactly?
How does the circle play it?
The ante's steep. Give me time.
The chit. The circle cashed out.
Back to the last hand.
Then we play the last hand. All three of us.
The last hand you ever dealt. Tell me.
Where's the game?
How does a dead man's hand beat a live one?
Not this hand. Not yet.
He drew his dead hand. We answered it. It's done.
